title: Sauerkraut
subtitle: Fermented white cabbage
excerpt: Shredded white cabbage lacto-fermented in its own brine with just salt. The fermentation takes one to four weeks at room temperature and produces a sharp, crunchy, tangy preserve that keeps for months in the fridge.

recipe.sourceNotes: Lacto-fermented cabbage appears across Central and Eastern European, German, Korean (kimchi), and East Asian traditions. The German name sauerkraut (sour cabbage) is the most familiar in English. Fermented cabbage is one of the oldest preserved foods in the world.

recipeTools.notes: A 1-litre jar with a wide mouth. Sterilise before use.

content.text: Sauerkraut is white cabbage fermented in its own brine with only salt. There is no vinegar and no cooking. The salt draws water out of the cabbage, which creates the brine the cabbage ferments in. The fermentation takes one to four weeks depending on the temperature of your kitchen and how sour you want the result. It keeps for months once it is in the fridge.

items.preparation: outer leaves removed, core discarded, finely shredded

content.text: Weigh the shredded cabbage into a large bowl. Sprinkle over the salt. Massage and squeeze the cabbage firmly with your hands for 5 to 10 minutes until it softens significantly, goes glossy, and has released a good amount of liquid. Add the caraway seeds if using.
Pack the cabbage tightly into a clean 1-litre jar, pressing it down firmly so the liquid rises to cover the cabbage. The cabbage must be submerged in its brine at all times.
If the liquid does not cover the cabbage after packing, make extra brine with 1 teaspoon of salt dissolved in 200 ml cold water and top up the jar.

Weigh the cabbage down with a small zip-lock bag filled with brine, or a small glass jar that fits inside, to keep it below the liquid. Cover the jar loosely with a cloth or a lid that is not sealed tight, to allow gas to escape.

Leave at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, for 1 to 4 weeks. Check daily and press the cabbage back down if it rises above the brine. Taste from day 7 onwards. It is ready when it has reached the sourness you like.

Once ready, seal the jar and transfer to the fridge. It will keep for up to 6 months. The fermentation slows to almost nothing in the cold but does not stop entirely, so the flavour continues to develop gradually.
White scum or foam on the surface: this is normal and harmless. Skim it off.
Mould growing on the cabbage above the brine: discard any mouldy cabbage. The submerged cabbage is still fine. Make sure to keep all the cabbage below the brine level from now on.
Not sour after a week: the kitchen is probably cool. Move to a slightly warmer spot, or simply wait longer.
